cls: Antilipemic / B-vitamin (niacin, vitamin B3) - broad-spectrum lipid-modifying agent
pharm: Niacin (nicotinic acid) at pharmacologic (gram) doses reduces hepatic VLDL and LDL production and is the most effective available agent for raising HDL cholesterol; it also lowers triglycerides and lipoprotein(a). Distinct from its vitamin role, the lipid effect is partly mediated by inhibition of adipocyte lipolysis, while the characteristic flushing is prostaglandin-mediated.
quick: Extended-release (Niaspan): titrate to 1000-2000 mg once daily at bedtime
Take ER at bedtime with a low-fat snack; avoid hot drinks, alcohol, spicy food around dosing
Lipid-lowering doses not recommended in pregnancy; vitamin doses are safe
Avoid pharmacologic doses; vitamin-level intake acceptable
Use caution; not well studied in severe renal impairment
Contraindicated in active liver disease or unexplained transaminase elevation
Avoid - worsens flushing and adds to hepatotoxicity
LFTs, glucose/HbA1c, uric acid, lipids, CK if myopathy symptoms
summary: Nicotinic acid (niacin) is a B-complex vitamin that, at pharmacologic gram-level doses, is a broad lipid-modifying agent: it lowers LDL cholesterol and triglycerides and raises HDL cholesterol more than any other drug. The FDA-approved prescription extended-release product (Niaspan) is indicated to reduce elevated cholesterol and triglycerides and is dosed once daily at bedtime with titration to limit adverse effects. The two dominant safety issues are flushing - a prostaglandin-mediated cutaneous reaction that is the leading cause of discontinuation, mitigated by aspirin 30 minutes before dosing, bedtime administration with a low-fat snack, slow titration, and avoiding hot drinks, alcohol, and spicy food - and hepatotoxicity, which is more frequent and more severe with sustained-release/extended-release formulations and requires LFT monitoring. Niacin also causes hyperglycemia, hyperuricemia/gout, and myopathy (particularly when combined with statins). Immediate-release (IR) and extended-release (ER) products are not interchangeable on a milligram basis.
indications: Adjunct to diet to reduce elevated total cholesterol, LDL cholesterol, apolipoprotein B, triglycerides, and to increase HDL cholesterol in primary hyperlipidemia and mixed dyslipidemia
Adjunct to diet for severe hypertriglyceridemia to reduce the risk of pancreatitis

In combination with a bile acid sequestrant to slow progression or promote regression of atherosclerotic disease in patients with coronary disease and hypercholesterolemia (historical/label combination indications)
Treatment and prevention of niacin (vitamin B3) deficiency / pellagra at vitamin-level doses

dosage.d: Start 500 mg at bedtime; increase by no more than 500 mg every 4 weeks to a usual maintenance of 1000-2000 mg once daily; max 2000 mg/day
dosage.n: Take with a low-fat snack; do not crush, chew, or split tablets; do not substitute mg-for-mg with IR niacin

dosage.d: Start 250 mg once daily with the evening meal; titrate gradually to 1.5-3 g/day in 2-3 divided doses (max ~6 g/day)
dosage.t: Two to three times daily with meals
dosage.n: More flushing but lower hepatotoxicity per gram than sustained-release forms

dosage.t: About 30 minutes before each niacin dose

dosage.d: 50-100 mg up to several times daily (deficiency); RDA ~14-16 mg/day
dosage.n: Vitamin replacement doses, far below lipid-modifying doses

admin: Take the extended-release tablet once daily at bedtime with a low-fat snack; swallow whole and do not break, crush, or chew
Premedicate with aspirin 325 mg or an NSAID about 30 minutes before the dose to reduce flushing
Avoid taking with hot beverages, alcohol, or spicy foods near dosing, as these worsen flushing
Titrate the dose slowly to build tolerance to flushing and limit hepatic and metabolic effects
Do NOT switch between immediate-release, sustained-release, and extended-release products on an equivalent milligram basis - re-titrate when changing formulation
If therapy is interrupted for an extended period, restart at a low dose and re-titrate
moa: Niacin modifies lipids by several mechanisms. In adipose tissue it inhibits hormone-sensitive lipase (partly via the GPR109A/HCA2 receptor), reducing free fatty acid mobilization to the liver and thereby decreasing hepatic triglyceride synthesis and VLDL secretion, which lowers LDL. It also inhibits hepatic diacylglycerol acyltransferase-2 and increases the rate of intracellular apolipoprotein B degradation. Niacin reduces clearance of HDL/apo A-I, raising HDL cholesterol, and lowers lipoprotein(a). Flushing is mediated by activation of GPR109A on cutaneous Langerhans/immune cells, stimulating prostaglandin D2 and E2 release, which causes cutaneous vasodilation - the basis for using aspirin/NSAIDs as premedication. Its vitamin function (as a precursor of NAD/NADP coenzymes) is separate from these pharmacologic lipid effects.

absolute: Active liver disease or unexplained, persistent elevations in hepatic transaminases
Known hypersensitivity to niacin or any product component
relative: Diabetes mellitus or impaired glucose tolerance (worsens glycemic control)
Unstable angina or acute MI phase (especially with vasodilators/nitrates)
History of jaundice, hepatobiliary disease, or peptic ulcer
monitor: Creatine kinase if muscle symptoms (myopathy, particularly with statins)
Platelet count and signs of bleeding with high doses

preg: Niacin at recommended dietary (vitamin) intakes is safe and necessary in pregnancy. However, the lipid-modifying gram-level doses have not been studied for safety in pregnancy and should generally not be used; lipid lowering can usually be deferred until after pregnancy. Use pharmacologic doses only if clearly needed (e.g., severe hypertriglyceridemia threatening pancreatitis) and the benefit justifies the risk.
lact: Niacin is a normal milk constituent at physiologic levels. Pharmacologic lipid-lowering doses are excreted into milk and could theoretically cause adverse effects in the infant; avoid high-dose niacin while breastfeeding or discontinue nursing. Vitamin-level intake during lactation is appropriate.
renal: Use with caution in renal impairment; niacin and its metabolites are renally excreted and there is limited study in severe renal disease. Hyperuricemia from niacin may be more problematic in patients with impaired renal function. Monitor uric acid and renal parameters.
hepatic: Hepatotoxicity is a major concern and is more frequent and more severe with sustained-release/extended-release formulations than with immediate-release niacin, including cases of fulminant hepatitis. Niacin is contraindicated in active liver disease or unexplained persistent transaminase elevations. Obtain baseline LFTs and monitor periodically (e.g., before initiation, every 6-12 weeks during the first year, then periodically). Discontinue if transaminases exceed about 3 times the upper limit of normal or if signs of hepatic dysfunction develop. Switching between formulations on a mg-for-mg basis can precipitate severe hepatotoxicity.

major: HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors (statins) - increased risk of myopathy and rhabdomyolysis
Other hepatotoxic drugs - additive liver injury
moderate: Antihypertensives, nitrates, and other vasodilators - additive hypotension/flushing
Insulin and oral antidiabetics - niacin raises glucose and may increase requirements
Bile acid sequestrants (colestipol, cholestyramine) - bind niacin; separate dosing by 4-6 hours
Anticoagulants/antiplatelets - high-dose niacin can reduce platelet count and prolong PT, increasing bleeding risk
minor: Uricosuric/antigout drugs - niacin raises uric acid and may blunt their effect
interactions.food: Take extended-release niacin with a low-fat snack; high-fat meals are not required and hot foods may worsen flushing. Avoid taking with hot beverages or spicy food around dosing.
interactions.alcohol: Avoid alcohol near dosing - it increases flushing and pruritus and adds to the risk of hepatotoxicity.
interactions.diagnostics: Niacin can cause false elevations in some urine catecholamine assays (fluorometric methods) and in urine glucose tests (Benedict reagent / copper-based). Monitor for elevated transaminases, glucose, and uric acid.

common: Flushing (warmth, redness, itching, tingling of face/neck)
serious: Hepatotoxicity (especially extended/sustained-release), including hepatitis and rare fulminant hepatic failure
emergency: Signs of hepatic failure (jaundice, confusion, coagulopathy)
Rhabdomyolysis (severe muscle pain, weakness, dark urine)

monitoring: Liver function tests at baseline and periodically (e.g., every 6-12 weeks in the first year, then periodically), especially with ER/SR products
Fasting blood glucose and HbA1c, particularly in patients with or at risk for diabetes
Lipid panel to assess response and guide titration
Creatine kinase if muscle pain or weakness occurs, especially with concurrent statins
Platelet count and signs of bleeding at high doses
counsel: Flushing - warmth and redness of the face and neck - is common, usually harmless, and tends to lessen over the first weeks; do not stop the medicine because of it
Take an aspirin (325 mg) or ibuprofen about 30 minutes before your dose to reduce flushing, if your doctor approves
Take the extended-release tablet at bedtime with a low-fat snack; swallow it whole and do not crush, chew, or split it
Avoid alcohol, hot drinks, and spicy foods around the time you take your dose, since they make flushing worse
Do not switch between different niacin brands or release forms on your own - the strengths are not interchangeable and switching can harm your liver
Tell your doctor about yellowing skin or eyes, dark urine, severe stomach pain, muscle pain or weakness, or unusual tiredness
If you have diabetes, check your blood sugar more closely, as niacin can raise it
Over-the-counter 'niacin' supplements at these high doses are still drugs - use only under medical supervision and have your blood tests done
pk: Flushing within 30 min to 1 h of a dose; lipid effects develop over weeks of titration
IR Tmax ~30-60 min; ER Tmax ~4-5 h
Short (~20-60 min for the parent), with dose-dependent, saturable hepatic metabolism
ER once-daily dosing; IR requires divided daily dosing
Store at room temperature ~20-25 C; protect from moisture; keep tightly closed
pearls: Niacin is the most effective drug for raising HDL and also lowers LDL, triglycerides, and Lp(a) - but large outcome trials (AIM-HIGH, HPS2-THRIVE) did not show added cardiovascular benefit when added to statins, and combination niacin-statin use has declined
Flushing is prostaglandin-mediated: pretreat with aspirin/NSAID 30 min before, dose at bedtime with a low-fat snack, titrate slowly, and avoid hot drinks/alcohol/spicy food
Hepatotoxicity is worse with sustained-release/extended-release forms - never switch formulations milligram-for-milligram; re-titrate from a low dose
Monitor for the metabolic trio: hyperglycemia, hyperuricemia/gout, and myopathy (especially with statins)
Immediate-release flushes more but is comparatively less hepatotoxic per gram than older sustained-release products
Distinguish vitamin (mg) dosing for pellagra from pharmacologic (gram) lipid dosing - the adverse effects are dose-dependent
missed: If you miss a dose of extended-release niacin, skip it and take your next dose at the usual bedtime; do not take two doses together. If you have stopped taking niacin for several days or longer, do not restart at your previous dose - contact your healthcare provider, as you may need to restart at a low dose and titrate up again to avoid severe flushing and other effects.
overdose: Overdose may cause severe flushing, pruritus, gastrointestinal distress, hypotension, hyperglycemia, and, with chronic high doses or sustained-release products, hepatotoxicity. There is no specific antidote. Treatment is symptomatic and supportive: support blood pressure and hydration, manage flushing, and monitor liver function, glucose, and uric acid. Standard gastric decontamination may be considered after a recent large ingestion.
